title: The sower (Matthew 13:1–23)
hook: seed on the path, the rocks, the thorns, and the good ground
tomorrow: the mustard seed and the yeast

segments.voice: Last week ended with the storm and three words to the sea: peace, be still. Now a new week: the stories he told.

The same lake, a calmer day. So many people have come to hear Jesus that he gets into a boat, pushes out a little, and sits down to teach, while the crowd stands on the shore. Instead of a lecture, he tells a story about farming, from the fields around that lake. In the Douay-Rheims: "Behold the sower went forth to sow." A man walks across a field, scattering seed by the handful. Some falls on the path. Some on rocky ground. Some among thorns. And some on good ground. That's almost the whole story.
screen: `A BOAT FOR A PULPIT.` → `A SOWER GOES OUT TO SOW.` → `FOUR KINDS OF GROUND.`

segments.voice: Today's word names this kind of story: parable. In Greek, parabolē: para, beside, and ballein, to throw. A story thrown down beside something, so you can compare them: an everyday picture laid next to the kingdom of God. A parable doesn't explain itself. It ends, and you're left holding it. Jesus ends this one: "He that hath ears to hear, let him hear." Now the four grounds. Seed on the path gets snatched by birds before it can sink in. Seed on rocks springs up fast in shallow soil, then withers in the sun, no roots. Seed among thorns grows, but the thorns grow too, and choke it. And seed on good ground bears fruit: some a hundredfold, some sixty, some thirty. Later his disciples ask what it means, and Matthew gives Jesus's explanation. The seed is the word of the kingdom. The path is someone who hears it and doesn't understand, and it's taken away. The rocks are someone who receives it with joy, but falls away when trouble comes. The thorns are the cares of the world and the lure of riches. The good ground hears, understands, and bears fruit. Notice the sower. He's not careful. He throws seed everywhere, even on the path, even on the rocks. Seed costs something, and he's generous with it anyway. Some readers say a single person can be all four grounds, on different days. Catholics hear this parable at Sunday Mass, and some use it to examine their hearts.
screen: `PARABOLĒ — THROWN BESIDE.` · `THE PATH, THE ROCKS, THE THORNS.` · `GOOD GROUND: A HUNDREDFOLD.` · `A SOWER WHO THROWS EVERYWHERE.` · then, large: `HE THAT HATH EARS TO HEAR, LET HIM HEAR.`

segments.voice: Without judging, just look at what kind of ground you are today: the path, too hurried for anything to sink in; the rocks, excited about something good but not rooted; the thorns, so full of worry and wanting there's no room; or a patch of good ground, soft and open. There may be some of each, so find the good patch, however small, and rest there. If you pray, you can ask God to make your ground good.
Parable. From the Greek for thrown beside: an everyday story laid next to the kingdom of God. Today's word.
Your line: be good ground. Whatever the soil, the sower still scatters the seed. Day forty-three, planted.

original.note: Greek: a comparison, literally something thrown beside. The word behind parable.

trapdoor: what you thought: a parable is a story with a moral.
what it means: an everyday picture laid beside the kingdom of God, that doesn't explain itself: he that hath ears, let him hear.
what a scholar hears: parabolē, from para and ballein, to throw beside. Matthew also gives Jesus's own explanation, ground by ground.

notes: Douay-Rheims wording of Matthew 13:3 and 13:9 given from memory; confirm.
Etymology of parabolē (para + ballein): standard; confirm.
'A hundredfold was an astonishing harvest': ancient yields are debated (often cited as tenfold typical); stated generally. Confirm.
The sower 'throws everywhere': some scholars note sowing before plowing in ancient Palestine; not mentioned.
Sunday Mass in summer (15th Sunday in Ordinary Time, Year A): confirm.
